answer_choices: High-sensitivity cardiac troponin
Exercise treadmill stress test
CT coronary angiography
D-dimer
Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy
blind_packets.lead_in: In addition to the electrocardiogram, which investigation is most important to obtain now?
blind_packets.stem: A 58-year-old man presents to the emergency department after 45 minutes of central chest pressure radiating to the left arm, accompanied by sweating and nausea. The discomfort began while he was walking uphill and settled about 20 minutes before arrival. He has hypertension and smokes. He is comfortable at rest. Heart rate is 78 beats/min, blood pressure 142/86 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths/min, oxygen saturation 97% on room air. Cardiac and respiratory examination is unremarkable, the chest wall is not tender, and there is no leg swelling. A 12-lead electrocardiogram shows sinus rhythm with no ST-segment or T-wave abnormality.

answer_choices: Fitness to drive is judged on his symptoms and his response to treatment rather than on the severity score alone, and the provincial licensing authority makes any restriction decision; in the meantime he should avoid alcohol and sedating sleep aids before bed and work on weight, smoking and regular sleep timing.

The apnea-hypopnea index recorded on his sleep study determines by itself whether he is permitted to drive, irrespective of how sleepy he feels, whether he has had a near-miss, or how well he responds to treatment.
Losing weight and sleeping on his side will cure his obstructive sleep apnea, so once he has made those two changes he will need no device, no prescription, and no further sleep-medicine follow-up.

A drink in the evening or his over-the-counter sleep aid will deepen his sleep and so reduce his daytime sleepiness, and he can go on using either of them while he waits for his treatment to be arranged.
Because he holds a private rather than a commercial licence, no driving restriction can ever apply to him and the provincial licensing authority has no role in a case like his.
blind_packets.lead_in: Which counselling statement is most appropriate?
blind_packets.stem: A 48-year-old man in Ontario has just been diagnosed with obstructive sleep apnea. He reports loud snoring, witnessed apneas and marked daytime sleepiness, and describes drifting across a lane on the highway last month before a passenger woke him. He holds a standard non-commercial driver's licence and does not drive for work. He drinks two or three alcoholic drinks in the evening most nights, takes an over-the-counter sleep aid, smokes, and has gained 12 kg over five years. He asks whether he is allowed to drive and what he can do himself while treatment is being arranged.

answer_choices: Supportive care with attention to feeding and hydration and repeated clinical assessment, without routine bronchodilators or corticosteroids
Regular nebulised salbutamol every four hours, continued while the wheeze persists
A single dose of oral dexamethasone, given now to reduce her airway inflammation
A seven-day course of oral amoxicillin, started now to cover a bacterial chest infection
Supplemental oxygen by nasal cannula, started now and continued until her wheeze settles
blind_packets.lead_in: Which is the most appropriate management?
blind_packets.stem: A previously healthy 7-month-old infant is brought to the emergency department in February. Three days of clear rhinorrhoea, cough and low-grade fever have been followed today by noisy breathing. This is her first episode of wheezing. She is alert and consolable. Temperature is 37.8 degrees Celsius, respiratory rate 52 breaths/min, heart rate 140 beats/min, oxygen saturation 94% on room air. There is mild subcostal indrawing, and the chest has widespread wheeze and fine crackles without focal findings. She has taken about three-quarters of her usual feed volumes and has had four wet nappies in the past day.

answer_choices: Untreated severe hyperbilirubinaemia can injure the brain, and the decision to treat depends on the measured bilirubin interpreted against the infant's age in hours, gestational age and neurotoxicity risk factors
The bilirubin level is the test that confirms biliary atresia, and it is needed today because surgical referral for that condition is time-critical
The bilirubin level determines whether breastfeeding must be stopped permanently, and the decision has to be made before the milk supply is established
The bilirubin level is the test used to diagnose neonatal sepsis, and sepsis must be identified today in a newborn who is feeding poorly and is hard to rouse
Jaundice at this age is always physiological and resolves without treatment, so the measurement is taken only to document the visit rather than to change what is done
blind_packets.lead_in: Which explanation best states why the bilirubin must be measured without delay?
blind_packets.stem: A term newborn is brought to the clinic on day five of life because she is feeding poorly and is difficult to rouse for feeds. She is exclusively breastfed and has lost 9% of her birth weight. She is afebrile and her vital signs are normal. She is visibly jaundiced over the face, chest, abdomen and thighs. The physician arranges immediate measurement of the bilirubin, and the parents ask why a blood test is needed today rather than at the scheduled visit next week.

answer_choices: Admit for haemodynamic stabilisation with intravenous access and fluid resuscitation, urgent haemoglobin measurement with treatment of severe anaemia, and treatment directed at controlling the bleeding
Prescribe tranexamic acid and arrange review at or shortly after her next period
Prescribe a non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug and arrange review in three months
Arrange insertion of a levonorgestrel intrauterine system at the next available outpatient appointment
Arrange an outpatient endometrial biopsy before any treatment is started
blind_packets.lead_in: Which is the most appropriate immediate management?
blind_packets.stem: A 27-year-old woman presents to the emergency department with heavy menstrual bleeding. Her periods have been heavy for about a year, but today she has soaked through a pad every hour for the past six hours and has passed large clots. She feels light-headed on standing. Heart rate is 118 beats/min, blood pressure 88/54 mmHg lying and lower on standing, and she is pale with cool peripheries. A urine pregnancy test is negative. Abdominal examination is soft and non-tender; on speculum examination there is active bleeding from the cervical os and no cervical or vaginal lesion.

answer_choices: Blood group and antibody screen
Group B streptococcus vaginal-rectal swab
Glucose challenge test for gestational diabetes
Fetal fibronectin swab
blind_packets.lead_in: Which investigation belongs to that routine baseline panel?
blind_packets.stem: A 26-year-old woman in her first pregnancy attends her family physician for her initial prenatal visit in the first trimester. She is well, takes no medication other than a folic-acid-containing prenatal vitamin, and has no personal or family history of note. A baseline history is taken and a physical examination performed, and the physician then orders the routine baseline laboratory panel offered to all pregnant patients at this visit.

answer_choices: Menopausal hormone therapy, after reviewing her individual contraindications and the balance of benefits and risks with her
Compounded bioidentical hormone preparations prepared by a compounding pharmacy
Lifestyle measures alone, with review in one year
A non-hormonal prescription alternative, because hormone therapy is contraindicated once menopause has occurred
Deferring all treatment until a further year of amenorrhoea has passed
blind_packets.lead_in: Which is the most appropriate first-line option to discuss with her?
blind_packets.stem: A 52-year-old woman attends her family physician. Her last menstrual period was 14 months ago. For the past year she has had eight to ten hot flushes a day and drenching night sweats that wake her repeatedly, and she is exhausted and struggling at work. She has no history of breast cancer, venous thromboembolism, coronary artery disease, stroke, liver disease or unexplained vaginal bleeding, and there is no family history of breast cancer. Blood pressure is 118/74 mmHg and body mass index is 24 kg/m2. She takes no medication. She asks what will most reliably relieve her symptoms.

answer_choices: Non-contrast CT of the head
MRI of the brain
Skull radiographs
CT angiography of the head and neck
No imaging, with clinical observation and reassessment in six hours
blind_packets.lead_in: Which imaging investigation is most appropriate now?
blind_packets.stem: A 62-year-old man is brought to the emergency department one hour after falling down a flight of stairs and striking his head. Bystanders report he was unresponsive for about a minute. He takes an oral anticoagulant for atrial fibrillation. His airway is clear, breathing is unlaboured and circulation is stable. He is drowsy but rousable, repeatedly asks the same questions, and has a boggy right parietal haematoma. Pupils are equal and reactive and there is no focal limb weakness.

answer_choices: Start a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor and review the response
Start clonazepam as ongoing maintenance treatment
Prescribe lorazepam to be taken before anticipated stressful situations as her only ongoing treatment
Start zopiclone at night and treat the anxiety only if her sleep does not improve
Prescribe propranolol as her only ongoing treatment
blind_packets.lead_in: Which is the most appropriate initial pharmacological management?
blind_packets.stem: A 29-year-old woman has had ten months of excessive, difficult-to-control worry about her work, finances and her family's health, with restlessness, fatigue, poor concentration, irritability and disturbed sleep. She is missing deadlines and has stopped meeting friends. She drinks little alcohol, uses no other substances, has no depressive episode and no suicidal ideation, and physical examination and screening bloodwork are normal. A diagnosis of generalized anxiety disorder is made. Cognitive behavioural therapy is offered and discussed; she declines psychological treatment for now and asks to start a medication.

answer_choices: Explain that a daily benzodiazepine is not the first-line ongoing treatment, and recommend starting an antidepressant of the serotonin reuptake inhibitor class at a low dose, cautioning that anxiety can increase transiently before it improves.
Agree to continue the lorazepam indefinitely as his main ongoing treatment and add nothing further.
Recommend starting the antidepressant at a full therapeutic dose immediately, so that the benefit begins as quickly as possible.
Explain that medication has no role in panic disorder and that the attacks will settle on their own with time.
Explain that benzodiazepines are unsafe in panic disorder and must never be used at all.
blind_packets.stem: A 34-year-old man has had six months of recurrent unexpected panic attacks with palpitations, breathlessness and a fear of dying, persistent worry about further attacks, and increasing avoidance of public transport. Cardiac and thyroid investigations were normal and panic disorder has been diagnosed. Two weeks ago a walk-in clinic gave him a short supply of lorazepam. He tells his family physician that it works within minutes and asks to stay on it as his ongoing treatment.

answer_choices: Carry out a suicide risk assessment now and arrange urgent care to establish his safety before other treatment proceeds
Refer him for trauma-focused psychotherapy at the next available appointment
Start a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor and review him in four weeks
Give advice on sleep and nightmares and review him in three months
Refer him for a non-urgent outpatient psychiatry assessment
blind_packets.lead_in: Which is the most appropriate immediate next step?
blind_packets.stem: A 41-year-old man has post-traumatic stress disorder following a motor vehicle collision a year ago, with nightmares, intrusive memories, hypervigilance and avoidance of driving. He attends a scheduled family practice appointment to discuss treatment. During the visit he says that for the past week he has been thinking about ending his life, that he has worked out how he would do it, that he has the means at home, and that he does not think he can go on.

answer_choices: Offer the patient time alone, explain to both of them what will be kept confidential and the circumstances in which the physician would have to disclose, and assess the patient's capacity for the specific decisions at hand
Decline to see the patient alone at any point in the visit, on the basis that a patient under the age of 16 must always be seen with a parent present
See the patient alone for part of the visit, but agree in advance with the mother that the content of that private conversation will be reported back to her in full
Assure the patient, before the private part of the visit begins, that nothing she says will ever be disclosed to her mother or to anyone else under any circumstances
Defer any confidential discussion, and any assessment of her capacity to make her own decisions, until the patient reaches the age of 18
blind_packets.lead_in: Which response best reflects appropriate practice?
blind_packets.stem: A 15-year-old attends a family practice appointment with her mother because of three months of fatigue. She answers questions briefly and looks at her mother before each reply. When the physician suggests spending part of the visit with the patient alone, the mother objects and says that as the parent she expects to be told everything her daughter says.
